title: Integer Optimization II: Scheduling, Location & the Midterm Case
subtitle: Set covering, workforce scheduling, and Google's CP-SAT solver — plus the midterm case launches: your team takes on retail replenishment optimization

objectives.title: Recognize the three discrete workhorse patterns
objectives.description: Formulate set covering, workforce scheduling, and knapsack models, and spot them hiding inside real staffing, location, and selection problems.

objectives.title: Solve scheduling problems with OR-Tools CP-SAT
objectives.description: Build a constraint programming model in Google's CP-SAT solver and understand when CP-SAT beats a MIP formulation for scheduling and feasibility-heavy problems.

objectives.title: Learn from a production replenishment system
objectives.description: Break down how ECCO Shoes automates roughly 300,000 monthly replenishment orders across 536 stores — and use it as the blueprint for your midterm case.

objectives.title: Launch the midterm case with a working plan
objectives.description: Leave tonight with your team formed, the retail replenishment case understood, and a concrete modeling plan for the November 4 deliverable.

agenda.title: Opening Story: ECCO's 300,000 Orders a Month
agenda.description: A 2026 Edelman finalist that looks exactly like your midterm case: ECCO Shoes automated store replenishment with optimization.
bulletPoints: The scale: ~300,000 replenishment orders per month across 536 stores, automated end to end
The payoff: several million euros in annual savings — from a decision that used to be spreadsheets and gut feel
Why replenishment is an integer problem: whole cartons, minimum order quantities, yes/no shipment decisions

agenda.title: Set Covering & Workforce Scheduling
agenda.description: The pattern behind fire stations, delivery zones, and every staff roster: cover all the demand with the fewest (or cheapest) resources.
bulletPoints: Set covering: binary selection so every demand point is covered by at least one chosen facility
Shift scheduling as covering: each hour of demand covered by enough overlapping shifts
Knapsack recap from Homework #5: same binaries, budget constraint instead of covering constraints

agenda.title: Meet CP-SAT: A Different Kind of Solver
agenda.description: Google's award-winning constraint programming solver — free, fast, and built for scheduling logic that is clumsy in MIP.
bulletPoints: CP-SAT thinks in constraints and feasibility, not LP relaxations — a different engine than branch & bound over LPs
Native modeling of logic: AddBoolOr, OnlyEnforceIf, interval variables for shifts and tasks
Rule of thumb: heavy logical structure and scheduling — try CP-SAT; heavy continuous costs and flows — stay with Gurobi

agenda.title: Break
agenda.description: Caffeinate — fittingly, you spend the next block scheduling the people who make the coffee.

agenda.title: Hands-On: Barista Shift Scheduling with CP-SAT
agenda.description: Teams schedule a week of barista shifts at a campus café: cover hourly demand, respect availability and max-shift rules, minimize labor cost.
bulletPoints: Binary assignment variables: barista b works shift s, or not
Coverage constraints per time block, plus rest rules via boolean logic
Solve, print the roster, then break it: add a Friday-evening demand spike and watch CP-SAT re-plan

agenda.title: MIDTERM CASE LAUNCH: Retail Replenishment Optimization
agenda.description: The main event. Teams receive the midterm case — a multi-store retail replenishment problem in the spirit of ECCO — due Session 9, November 4.
bulletPoints: The case: decide weekly replenishment quantities for a store network under warehouse capacity, minimum order quantities, and service-level requirements
Deliverables: working Colab model, a 5-page decision memo for the COO, and a 10-minute team presentation on November 4
Tonight: form teams of 3-4, read the case brief together, and draft your decision variables and constraints before you leave

agenda.title: Wrap-Up & Next Steps
agenda.description: Case logistics, office hours for teams, and a preview of nonlinear optimization.
bulletPoints: This week's homework IS the case: get your data pipeline and first model draft running
Team check-ins available during office hours and by appointment
Next week: when the world stops being linear — portfolios, pricing, and curves

activities.title: Barista Shift Scheduling with CP-SAT
activities.description: The campus café needs a week of shifts covered: morning rush, midday, and evening blocks, each with a minimum barista count. Six baristas with different availability and wage rates. Build a CP-SAT model that covers every block, respects everyone's limits, and minimizes labor cost.

steps.title: Define assignment variables
steps.description: One BoolVar per (barista, shift) pair. This is the set-covering skeleton: rows are shifts to cover, columns are people who can cover them.

steps.title: Add coverage and availability constraints
steps.description: Each shift needs at least its required headcount; baristas only work shifts they are available for; nobody exceeds 5 shifts per week or works both closing and next-morning opening.

steps.title: Minimize cost and solve
steps.description: Objective: sum of wage times hours times assignment. Solve with CpSolver, check the status is OPTIMAL, and print a human-readable roster.

steps.title: Re-plan under a demand spike
steps.description: Friday evening now needs 3 baristas instead of 2. Re-solve and compare rosters — note how fast CP-SAT handles the change, and who absorbed the extra shift.

activities.discussionNote: Your café has 6 people and 15 shift blocks. ECCO's system makes ~300,000 replenishment decisions a month across 536 stores — same class of model, industrial scale, several million euros a year in savings. As you draft your midterm case model tonight, ask the ECCO question: which decisions are truly binary, which constraints are hard rules versus preferences, and what single objective would the COO actually sign off on?

takeaways.text: Set covering, scheduling, and knapsack are the three discrete patterns you will see everywhere: cover the demand, respect the person-level rules, spend the budget where it earns most.
CP-SAT is a genuinely different engine — logic-first, feasibility-driven, free — and it is often the right tool when scheduling rules get gnarly. Two solvers in your toolkit beats one.

The midterm case is live. ECCO turned this exact problem class into several million euros a year across 536 stores — your team has three weeks to show the same thinking on the retail replenishment case, due November 4.

homework.label: Midterm Case
homework.text: Midterm case work (in lieu of a numbered problem set): with your team, (1) finalize your team roster on the course site by Friday, (2) load the case data into Colab and produce summary statistics on store demand and warehouse capacity, and (3) draft your model skeleton — decision variables, objective, and at least four constraint families — as a one-page outline. Bring the outline to Session 8 for a 5-minute check-in with the instructor. Full deliverables (model, 5-page COO memo, 10-minute presentation) are due Session 9, November 4.

nextSession.title: Nonlinear Optimization: Portfolios, Pricing & Curves
nextSession.description: Linearity has taken us far, but risk is quadratic, demand curves bend, and prices interact. Next week we enter nonlinear optimization: Markowitz portfolios, revenue-maximizing pricing, and how modern solvers handle curvature — while your midterm case work continues in the background.
